did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 32 opens with a precise date: the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the first day of the month. On that date, Ezekiel received a prophecy concerning Pharaoh, king of Egypt.

Did you know? Pharaoh is described through a double image: as a lion among the nations and as a “sea monster,” a powerful creature in the waters that boasts about its rivers and fouls them with its feet.

Did you know? The LORD announces that He will spread a net over Pharaoh “in the assembly of many peoples,” and the peoples will draw him out of the waters in their net. This image portrays Egypt’s downfall as the result of the combined action of many nations.
Did you know? The fall of Egypt is described as an event of cosmic proportions: the heavens are covered, the stars are darkened, the sun is obscured by a cloud, and the moon does not give its light.

Did you know? Egypt’s downfall is meant to shock many peoples, even in lands unknown to Pharaoh and his people. Thus, the prophecy emphasizes that the disaster will be widely known and far-reaching in its effects.

Did you know? The chapter explicitly states that the sword coming against Egypt is the sword of the king of Babylon. Babylon is presented here as the instrument through which Egypt will meet its downfall.

Did you know? After the destruction of people and animals in the waters of Egypt, the land is described as devoid of human and animal movement: no human foot or animal hoof will disturb the waters again, and the rivers will become quiet and clear.

Did you know? The chapter’s second lament is delivered on another date: in the twelfth year, on the fifteenth day of the month. It concerns the descent of Egypt and mighty nations into “the depths of the earth,” an image of the place of the dead.

Did you know? Among the kingdoms mentioned in the realm of the dead is Elam, described together with its people as having fallen by the sword and bearing their shame after spreading terror in the land of the living.

Did you know? At the end, it is said that Pharaoh will lie among those slain by the sword, and that his terror—the fear he inspired—will be in the land of the living. Thus, the chapter portrays the end of Pharaoh’s reign of terror and the LORD’s supremacy over every human kingdom.
